1_which_grant_admits.defeating_case_driven: Revoking a revoke:authority grant that was itself the newest live match. The COMMITTED receipt cited the older live revoke:authority, never the target, and the target was absent from the live set afterwards. Separately, a node holding exactly one live revoke:authority is refused MISSING_PRECONDITION rather than being allowed to spend it on its own withdrawal; the same holds for the only grant:authority; and a second revoke:authority recorded at a scope that admits nothing does not satisfy the last-holder rule.
1_which_grant_admits.method: Built a 36-entry journal through the CLI including two effective revocations, replayed it with RecordService, folded authority-grant and authority-revocation myself in append order, and for each COMMITTED receipt compared its authority_grant_ids against the set I computed live at the position the check ran (strictly before the receipt's own emitted event) and at the receipt's own index.
1_which_grant_admits.not_covered_by_the_claim: Two COMMITTED receipts on every fresh node carry an empty authority_grant_ids: the bootstrap genesis pair, self-issued by the first caller to name the node. No grant admitted them. The claim's wording is satisfied by an empty citation, so a reader assuming 'every COMMITTED receipt names the grant that admitted it' would be wrong about the first two.
1_which_grant_admits.verdict: REPRODUCED, bounded to a single writer

2_one_fact_one_refusal_code.collapse_confirmed: archive-thread, close-session, withdraw-publication, read-thread and revoke answer a peer's record with exactly the code and message shape they give an absent one, differing only in the id the caller itself typed. The REFUSED receipts written to the journal are identical too: same event, same actor, same reason_code, same detail keys, and the only differing field is the subject the caller supplied.
2_one_fact_one_refusal_code.declared_but_not_measured: The check behind 'declared on every operation that can return it' is services/console/tests/test_declared_refusals.py, whose ABSENT_ID is a hand-maintained dict of eight operations, and the manifest-coverage case iterates that same dict. So the census is a declaration, not a measurement: a sixteenth BUILT operation that reads a record by id would answer UNKNOWN_RECORD and pass this suite untouched. It is currently correct - my own 19 probes, which include five operations that dict does not name, found no undeclared code - but the check cannot see an operation nobody adds to it.
2_one_fact_one_refusal_code.method: 19 CLI probes across every BUILT operation that names a record by id, against an absent id and against a record this store carries under node:peer, with the manifest read as bytes and the produced reason_code looked up in it here.
2_one_fact_one_refusal_code.two_surfaces_agree: ConsoleRoutes.call('read-thread', ...) and the CLI both answer an absent thread with UNKNOWN_RECORD. THREAD_UNKNOWN survives nowhere in the repository except as prose explaining its retirement and as a test asserting its absence.

3_discovery_refuses_readably.map_not_read_before_the_grant: An ungranted caller gets the identical NO_LIVE_GRANT answer for a path that does not exist, a path that is a directory, and the real map. Only after read:session scoped to the caller is minted do those three diverge into UNREADABLE, UNREADABLE and a successful answer. The declared-stale path is also behind the grant: `--stale` from an ungranted caller is NO_LIVE_GRANT, not MISSING_PRECONDITION.
3_discovery_refuses_readably.method: 439 capability-map inputs through the CLI: 3 path shapes (absent, a directory, the real map), 36 hand-built malformed maps covering every field projection.readable names plus wrong types at each, and 400 randomised deep mutations of the real map (seeded, 1-3 edits each, dropping keys and substituting 17 wrong-typed values at every depth).

4_authority_before_the_read.method: Ungranted probes on console.revoke and console.open-thread, comparing a real subject against an invented one and against a peer node's.
4_authority_before_the_read.result: All four answers are identical in exit code (2), outcome, reason_code (NO_LIVE_GRANT) and message text; the message names the capability and never the scope, the subject or its owner. Reading the source confirms the ordering: permits.withdraw calls require() before grant_record(), and threads.open_thread calls console.authorize() before console.channel().

findings_the_report_did_not_carry.finding: The manifest's own `note` opens 'Twelve operations are BUILT' while the same file declares 15 operations at standing BUILT and the note goes on to describe 'nine of the fifteen'. A stale sentence in the artifact the claim is about.

The CLI's stated contract - 'every command writes one JSON object to stdout, including refusals', 'exit codes: 0 committed, 2 refused, 3 unknown record, 1 usage error' - does not hold for an argparse usage error. A missing required flag, an unknown subcommand, no subcommand, and an out-of-choice --actor-kind each exit 2 with zero bytes on stdout and a usage message on stderr. Exit 2 is the code the module reserves for REFUSED, so a machine caller cannot tell a refusal from a malformed invocation by exit code. This is the same class the branch repaired one commit earlier for `--node BAD` (5228e83), which now correctly returns JSON at exit 1; the sibling entry point was left.

test_declared_refusals.py grades a declaration where it could measure. Its ABSENT_ID is a hand-kept dict of eight operations and the manifest-coverage case walks the same dict, so 'declared on every operation that can return it' is enforced against a list somebody maintains rather than against the operation set. Currently correct; blind to a new operation.

subject_claim.claim: Nine BUILT console operations declared a required authority and checked nothing; all nine are now guarded.
subject_claim.how: One fresh journal per probe so no earlier grant leaked in. For each of the 15 BUILT operations: call it over the CLI holding nothing, then mint exactly the grant contracts/capability-offices.json declares for that operation, then call it again.

what_a_reader_would_assume_the_claims_co: That a guarded operation means an authorised caller. It does not. Every principal in this service is a string the caller types, and the walk under known_gaps_checked_by_driving_them.identity takes a private thread with declared operations only.
That claim 1 holds with more than one process on the store. It is scoped to a single writer and says so; with two writers the digest chain itself breaks, which I reproduced.
That every COMMITTED receipt names the grant that admitted it. The two bootstrap genesis grants on every fresh node cite nothing.

That UNKNOWN_RECORD is the uniform answer for 'not carried by this node'. Three operations answer FOREIGN_NODE_RECORD once a grant has been shown, and because node names are unbounded that difference is a working cross-node existence oracle. KNOWN-GAPS records it on the node-identity row; the claims do not.
That guarding the declared operations guards the data. Three package exports return the same bytes to an in-process caller with no check, confirmed above.
That the discovery answer being complete means it is current. `freshness.verified` was null on every run here, and the answer says so itself.
